title: USS Abraham Lincoln Returns to San Diego After Historic, Grueling Combat Deployment
snippet: The aircraft carrier arrived in San Diego Bay following an 11-month mission in the Middle East marked by intense combat, high military honors, and political debate over crew conditions.
content:
SAN DIEGO — After nearly 11 months at sea marked by intense combat, extended deployments, and heightened political scrutiny, the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln pulled into its homeport at Naval Air Station North Island on Thursday morning.

Thousands of military families lined the shores of San Diego Bay, waving American flags and holding tearful reunions as the 1,092-foot supercarrier docked. The Lincoln spent more than 260 consecutive days at sea during its deployment to the Middle East—a record-setting streak that saw the crew play a frontline role in combat operations against Iran.

A Storied Mission and Political Fallout

Defense leaders touted the strike group's operational achievements. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew aboard the vessel on Wednesday to present the crew with the Presidential Unit Citation, the military's highest collective unit honor. According to Hegseth, the Lincoln strike group flew over 10,000 sorties, logged 23,000 flight hours, dropped 1.5 million pounds of ordnance, and sank 64 Iranian naval vessels during what he characterized as a 'generational mission.'

However, the carrier's extended deployment was not without controversy back home. Reports of severe shipboard conditions—including broken plumbing, food rationing, and mental health emergencies—sparked widespread debate in Washington. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirmed in late September that eight suicide attempts occurred within the strike group during the mission, prompting Democratic lawmakers, including Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., to request formal congressional hearings.

Administration officials, including President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Hegseth, forcefully dismissed reports of dire conditions aboard the ship, framing media coverage as an unfair distortion of a successful mission.

Sacrifice on the Home Front

For the nearly 6,000 sailors and Marines aboard, the nearly year-long tour was defined as much by personal isolation as by high-stakes operations. Operational security requirements and restricted Wi-Fi connectivity often cut off service members from news and communication with loved ones for extended periods.

Petty Officer Steven Rivas was among dozens of crew members who became parents while deployed. Due to strict communication blackouts during active operations, Rivas did not learn of his daughter Evie's birth until more than a week after she was delivered.

As crew members in crisp dress uniforms finally stepped off the gangway on Thursday to embrace waiting families, many expressed relief at stepping back onto American soil after one of the longest and most demanding naval deployments in modern U.S. history.
